title: Why Do the Wicked Prosper?
summary: Jeremiah takes God to court with the ancient question of why the wicked prosper while the land withers. God answers not with an explanation but with a harder assignment: if running with men has tired you, how will you race horses? God then laments that he has forsaken his own house and given his beloved to her enemies, and closes with a surprising promise that even Judah's hostile neighbors may be restored if they learn to swear by his name.
story: This chapter completes the first of Jeremiah's confessions, begun in 11:18. The plot at Anathoth has shown the prophet what faithfulness costs, and now he asks why God allows it. His question, and God's reply, prepare him for everything that follows in the book: persecution, imprisonment, and the fall of the city. The chapter then turns to God's own grief. The one who sends the judgment also mourns it, and Jeremiah's pain is set beside the pain of God. The last verses reach beyond Judah to the nations around it, the first hint that God's purpose in the exile includes not only uprooting but replanting, even for outsiders.
historical:
The chapter has no date. Its situation fits the reign of Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC), when Jeremiah's life was repeatedly in danger and when Judah's neighbors took advantage of its weakness. The “evil neighbors” of verse 14 likely include Edom, Moab, Ammon, and the Arameans; 2 Kings 24:2 records that raiding bands from Babylon, Aram, Moab, and Ammon were sent against Judah in Jehoiakim's last years. The land's mourning in verse 4 may point to a drought, a common disaster in a country that depended on seasonal rain, and one that chapter 14 describes directly.

The “thickets of the Jordan” (verse 5) were the dense jungle of tamarisk, willow, and reeds along the river's lower course. In biblical times it was home to wild animals, including lions (49:19), and was dangerous ground compared with the open, settled country. God's question means: if you falter where it is safe, what will you do in the wild.
cultural:
Jeremiah's opening words are courtroom language. He grants that God is righteous, the judge who cannot lose a case, and then asks to “contend” with him anyway, using the verb for bringing a legal complaint (riv). Israel's faith gave room for this. Abraham argued with God over Sodom (Genesis 18), Job demanded a hearing, and the psalmists asked why the wicked flourish (Psalm 73). Honest protest addressed to God was a form of faith, not its opposite.

The images of verses 7 to 13 come from farming and herding. God's “inheritance” is his people and land, the family estate in Israelite law that was never supposed to be sold out of the family. A “speckled bird of prey” may picture a bird of odd coloring that others attack, and the “shepherds” who trample the vineyard are rulers, native or foreign; in the ancient Near East kings were routinely called shepherds of their people. A vineyard took years to establish, so to trample one was to destroy a generation's work. Swearing “As surely as the LORD lives” (verse 16) was the ordinary way of taking an oath, and whose name a person swore by showed which god they trusted.
literary: The chapter moves in three steps. Verses 1 to 4 are Jeremiah's complaint, built like a psalm of lament with a confession of God's righteousness, a question, a description of the wicked, and a plea. Verses 5 to 13 are God's reply, first to Jeremiah (verses 5 and 6, a pair of rhetorical questions) and then a lament in God's own voice over his house, heaped with images: a lion, a bird of prey, a vineyard, a field, a failed harvest. The word “inheritance” occurs five times in the chapter and ties the sections together. Verses 14 to 17, in prose, use the key verbs of Jeremiah's call in 1:10: God will “uproot” (the word occurs five times here) and then build. The wordplay of verse 2 is also worth noticing: the wicked are planted and bear fruit, but God is near their lips and far from their hearts, literally their kidneys, the seat of inner feeling.

outline.t: Jeremiah's complaint: why do the wicked prosper?
God's answer: you must race with horses
God's lament over his forsaken inheritance
Uprooting and replanting for the neighbors

doctrines.note: The chapter does not solve the problem of why the wicked prosper. It shows a faithful man asking it openly and God answering by strengthening him for more, not by explaining everything.
God planted the wicked and will also uproot them. Their prosperity is real but temporary, and the chapter insists that the whole history of the nations remains in his hand.
Verses 15 and 16 promise compassion to Judah's enemies if they learn the ways of God's people. Even in the age of judgment the door stands open for the nations to be built into Israel.

words.note: Riv, to contend, argue, or bring a lawsuit. It is legal vocabulary: the prophets use its noun for God's case against Israel. Here the direction is reversed, and the prophet brings a case against God. That Jeremiah dares this, while confessing God's righteousness in the same breath, is a model of faith that argues rather than walks away.

Nachalah, inheritance, the family land passed down within a clan. It appears five times in this chapter. When God calls Israel “My inheritance” he speaks as a father about his own estate, which makes it all the more shocking that he has abandoned it (verse 7). In verses 14 and 15 the same word describes each nation's land, so the chapter's hope reaches beyond Israel.

Natash, to uproot or pull up, as a farmer pulls a plant. It is one of the six verbs of Jeremiah's commission (1:10: uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow, build, plant). Here it is used five times, but the chapter ends with a condition under which uprooted nations will be established, so the uprooting is not the last word.

christ: The chapter's final verses are among the Old Testament's early glimpses of the nations being gathered into God's people, a hope the prophets develop and the New Testament sees fulfilled when Gentiles are grafted into the people of God through Christ (Romans 11:17-24; Ephesians 2:11-22). The link is a promise that widens, not a detailed forecast. The chapter also joins the prophet's grief to God's own: God says he has handed “the love of My life” to her enemies. The New Testament shows God entering that grief in the flesh when Jesus weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44). And Jeremiah's betrayal by his own household (verse 6) belongs to a pattern Jesus names when he says a prophet is without honor in his hometown and among his own relatives (Mark 6:4).

hard.q: Why doesn't God answer Jeremiah's question about the prosperity of the wicked?
hard.a: Readers often feel that verse 5 dodges the question. Jeremiah asked why; God tells him things will get worse. There are several ways to read this. One is that God does answer indirectly: verses 7 to 13 show that judgment is coming, so the prosperity of the wicked is short-lived. Another is that the Bible deliberately leaves the question open, as Job and Ecclesiastes do, and that God meets Jeremiah with presence and a calling rather than a theory. A third notes that God treats Jeremiah as strong enough for a hard truth. None of these makes the question go away, and the chapter doesn't pretend it does. Its gift is that the question itself is allowed, voiced by a prophet, and preserved in Scripture.

questions: Jeremiah argued with God while confessing that God is righteous. Have you felt free to bring your hardest questions to God directly? What keeps people from doing that?
God's answer in verse 5 prepares Jeremiah for harder things. When has a difficult season turned out to be preparation for something heavier?
Verses 15 and 16 offer mercy to Judah's enemies. What does it say about God that his judgment on the nations leaves room for their restoration?
